name: Yellowish Grey
lede: Yellowish grey is a plain descriptive name that became a numbered standard: entry 13 among the greys in Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of Werner's colour list.

sections.title: A grey with a yellow lean
sections.body:
Yellowish grey is a descriptive name, and it is also a numbered standard. It is entry 13 among the greys in Patrick Syme's 1821 edition of *Werner's Nomenclature of Colours*, a list built to describe minerals, plants and animals [1][4]. Abraham Gottlob Werner began the list in 1774 with 54 names, and Syme enlarged it to 110 and painted a swatch for each [1].

The name is plain on purpose. Werner's lists sort greys by the hue they lean toward, so that yellowish grey sits beside [[bluish-grey]], [[greenish-grey]], [[pearl-grey]] and [[french-grey]] [2][4].

sections.title: Syme's recipe and examples
sections.body:
Syme gave it as a recipe: ash grey, with lemon yellow added and a very small amount of brown [4]. His three examples were the vent coverts of the "White Rump" (Baty's gloss: the hen harrier), the stems of the barberry, and the mineral common chalcedony [4]. Patrick Baty's modern edition pairs these with drawings from Gould's *Birds of Europe* (1832 to 1837), a botanical watercolour of 1765 and a mineral catalogue of 1797 [4].

Syme also used it as a building block for other colours. Two of his greens list it among the parts: oil green combines emerald green, lemon yellow, chesnut brown and yellowish grey, and mountain green takes emerald green, plenty of blue and a little yellowish grey [5]. A flat grey with a bit of yellow does the work of dulling a bright green into a natural one.

sections.title: Where the name spread
sections.body:
The term was not Syme's invention [2]. Yellowish grey appears in several of the colour lists that Baty tabulates, and in Syme's editions of both 1814 and 1821 [2][3]. Baty's index gives six page references for it, among them the lists of terms and the entry for the colour itself [6].

Outside the Werner tradition the plain words are common [7]. The dictionary entry for beige gives a light brown or yellowish grey, the entry for stone calls it a yellowish grey colour, and *fulvid* is an old term for reddish yellow, tawny or yellowish grey [7][8]. In those uses the phrase is a description, not a standard. Close modern names are [[beige]], [[stone]], [[taupe]], [[putty]] and [[tan]] [9].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
Our swatch is Werner's no. 13, taken from an aged scan, so it is approximate [9]. It is a light, soft olive-tan, lighter and yellower than most things called grey today [9]. Syme's plates have muted with age, and the original may have been fresher [1].

That matters for a colour defined by a recipe. A mix of ash grey, lemon yellow and brown is sensitive to the pigments chosen, and nothing in the lists fixes them [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive the colour appears in 3,537 of 23,781 paintings, about 15 per cent, within CIEDE2000 distance 6 and at least 5 per cent of the canvas [10]. That is common because it is the colour of aged paper, canvas and varnished lights, and 89 per cent of the matching area sits in the highlights [10]. Read this as photographed: museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment tests [10].

It is strongest in Dutch landscape and sea painting [10]. Willem van de Velde the Elder has 12 of 14 paintings in the match, including [[painting:rijks-20026834|Ships after the Battle]], where it covers 86 per cent of the picture [10]. Meindert Hobbema has 11 of 16 and Jan van Goyen 12 of 22 [10]. By century the rate rises from about 11 per cent in the 1500s to 17 per cent in the 1700s and 1800s [10].

The words nearest to it in the archive are sage, beige, tan, ash and khaki [10].
